Carl Ganter/Circle of Blue Posted in Water Policy A Big Blue Pivot for Water and the Environment Voters approve conservation measures and elect lawmakers to impede Trump’s attack on policy and programs. by Keith Schneider November 17, 2026 November 16, 2026 Share this article: Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Bluesky (Opens in new window) Bluesky Key Points: - Voters supported candidates and ballot measures to protect water, land, and communities. - Democratic governors and majorities in Congress and state Legislatures are poised to enact reforms and weaken White House-led attack on the environment. - Water quality activist Chris Jones lost his race for Iowa agriculture secretary but captured an even greater prize. At the state level, the most visible indicator of voter sentiment on the environment was the near total rejection of data center construction. Of the 41 measures up for votes across the country to curtail or halt data centers, just one in North Dakota failed. This AWS data center is under construction in New Carlisle, Indiana. ©J. Carl Ganter/Circle of Blue Election day was a glorious affirmation of America’s character. Along with casting aside bigotry and cruelty, especially satisfying was the support for referendums and candidates to protect water, land, and communities. The environment swung back big on November 3. Democratic lawmakers, many of whom campaigned on restricting data center development, will have new authority in the House and Senate to seriously weaken the White House-led attack on environmental policies and programs. While the president and his cabinet maintain executive authority, members of Congress decide agency budgets and can influence permitting decisions for big projects by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, Environmental Protection Agency, and other agencies. One clear example is how Congress can disrupt the Trump administration’s bid to rescind the 25-year-old rule protecting roadless wilderness on federal forest land , which the Agriculture Department proposed on August 18, 2026.
